title: Good tidings of great joy (Luke 2:8–20)
hook: the angel to the shepherds: fear not, a savior is born
tomorrow: now let me go in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, kataluma: a full guest room, and a baby laid in a manger at the edge of an emperor's world. Your line was not counted, but there.

Out in the fields near Bethlehem, a few shepherds are keeping watch over their flock by night. It's dark, and the job is mostly staying awake. Not people anyone would invite to a palace. Not people the emperor's census was thinking about. Then, in the King James Bible: "the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid. Terrified. The dark field suddenly blazing. And the angel's first words are ones Zechariah and Mary have already heard.

"Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." Every phrase is loaded. Good tidings means good news, the very thing the word gospel names, coming to shepherds, about a baby. To all people: not just the important ones. This day: tonight, not someday. And the sign isn't a palace or a crown: "Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." The sign is how ordinary he is. Then the sky fills with a multitude of angels praising God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." That line opens the Gloria, a hymn still sung in churches. Compare Bibles and the end of the line varies: the King James says good will toward men; other translations say peace among people with whom God is pleased. Then the shepherds do the simplest thing: "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." They find everything as they were told, spread the word, and people wonder at it. Then a quiet line: "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The shepherds broadcast; Mary treasures. Both are ways of receiving good news. And the shepherds go back to the same sheep, glorifying and praising God as they go.
screen: `THE SIGN IS HOW ORDINARY HE IS.`
then, large: `GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY, TO ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Find one piece of good news that's actually true, a friend's recovery, a kindness you saw, a baby born, a small win, and sit with it for a moment the way Mary pondered. Then picture the person who'd most like to hear it, someone surrounded by bad news lately, and imagine telling them the way the shepherds did, a little breathless, not polished. If you pray, give thanks for it first; if not, simply enjoy it before you share it.
Evangelist. The English word that comes from the angel's own verb, to announce good news, first spoken to shepherds in a dark field.
Your line: great joy for all people. Not just the important ones. Day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christians read the shepherds' story at Christmas, and the angels' song lives on in the Gloria, sung or said in Sunday worship in some churches, and in Christmas carols.

notes: Luke 2:14 variant: eudokia (nominative, 'good will toward men', Byzantine text behind the KJV) vs eudokias (genitive, 'among men of good will / with whom he is pleased', older manuscripts). Confirm the 'single letter' description.
Imperial use of 'good news' (euangelion) language, e.g. the Priene inscription on Augustus's birthday. Stated generally.
Shepherds' social status: the script avoids claiming they were despised (debated); says only 'not people anyone would invite to a palace'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fixes: the hook said the angel's first words to Mary were 'fear not' (her first words were 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured', 1:28; 'fear not' comes at 1:30), now 'the words Zechariah and Mary have already heard'; 'the root of the word gospel' was wrong for English (gospel comes from Old English, not the Greek verb), now 'what gospel means'. Also cut the manuscript 'single letter' claim (now a plain note that translations differ), 'emperors used that language', 'Luke's favorite word' (day 500 used semeron), 'for many centuries', and the invented 'cold night'; opener no longer 'Night shift' (day 519 opens on a night shift, day 510 on a watchman).
